newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: New EU treaty amounts to less than a tune up.
newsitem.headline: New EU treaty amounts to less than a tune up.

text.p: A 10,000 mile (km) tune up or simply a tyre change?

The European Union's Treaty of Amsterdam approved by EU leaders at their mid-year summit in the early hours of Wednesday was never supposed to be a radical overhaul of the 15-nation bloc's structures.
Even the often-quoted comment that it was to prepare the Union for its historic enlargement into eastern Europe was over stated.

Ordered up by the far more ground-breaking Maastricht Treaty, it was, as one Brussels diplomat famously described it, supposed to be just a pit stop, a tweak of the engine before more serious changes were thrust upon it.

But even by that standard, the treaty agreed in Amsterdam ended up as pretty thin gruel, drained of its substance by the demands of nation states in a negotiation remarkably lacking in the community drive the EU formally prides itself in.
The treaty was scattered with opt-outs, protocols and declarations.
Plans to beef up foreign and defence became commitments to further cooperation.
Majority voting, seen as essential to make the bloc work more efficiently, was extended only in minor areas.

To different extents Britain, Ireland, Germany, Denmark, Spain all demanded special treatment while a decision to defer the tough question of how much power EU states should have reflected a keen desire to protect national turf.
"We set our sights high but had to make do with something less ambitious," admitted European Commission President Jacques Santer, whose normal public state is unbridled optimism.
The vaunted Franco-German alliance, already strained over the new French government opposition to the austerity needed for monetary union, was hardly to be seen.
"It's the confirmation of two things," one EU diplomat said of the outcome. "A lack of political appetite to make serious changes and a lack of political leadership due to the change of landscape."
The French election, German domestic problems, British caution about Europe were all in play.

Officials said privately the leaders simply wanted to get the treaty behind them, in part to meet political demands at home, in part to concentrate on the main issue before them -- qualifying for the single currency.

They shrugged off worries that enlargement plans would suffer from the lack of institutional reform, but were under no illusions that anything had been achieved to bring the former Communist bloc closer.
"There is nothing in the new treaty that could endanger enlargement," said on government official. "But there is nothing that is going to make enlargement easier."
